title: You knit me together (Psalm 139)
hook: you know when I sit and rise; if I take the wings of morning, you are there

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the rivers of Babylon, harps hung on the willows. Your line was how can we sing here? Who did you think of, far from home? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

On a lot of refrigerators there's a small, grainy, black-and-white picture held up by a magnet. You have to squint. A curve that might be a spine. A blur that might be a hand. The people who put it there can tell you exactly which smudge is the nose. Before anyone has held this child, before anyone knows its laugh, it is already known, already loved, already the most looked-at picture in the house. Three thousand years before ultrasound, a psalm imagined that same hidden beginning, and claimed that someone was watching it closely. Today, Psalm one hundred thirty-nine, the psalm of being known all the way down.
screen: `A GRAINY PICTURE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `KNOWN BEFORE BEING HELD.` → `KNOWN ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off." Sitting down, getting up, a thought before it's finished. Then the writer tries to imagine getting away. "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Up to heaven: you're there. Down to the grave: you're there. "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me." The wings of the morning: fly as fast as the dawn moves across the sky, all the way to the far edge of the sea. Still held. Then the psalm goes inward, to the womb. The King James says, "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb." The Hebrew verb can mean cover, or weave together, which is why many later translations say knit. Two verses on, the writer says he was "curiously wrought" in secret, a phrase for embroidery, colored thread worked by hand. And in between, the line: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Fearfully here means with awe, the way you'd handle something precious. Here's a twist worth knowing. Near the end, the psalm turns angry: the writer wants God to slay the wicked. And then, right after, he stops and turns the searchlight on himself: "Search me, O God, and know my heart." See if there's any wicked way in me. A psalm that starts with being searched ends by asking for it.
screen: `MY DOWNSITTING AND MINE UPRISING` · `THE WINGS OF THE MORNING` · `WOVEN, EMBROIDERED IN SECRET` · `SEARCH ME, O GOD` · then, large: `I AM FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: place your hand on your heart. Gently, flat, so you can feel it beating. Close your eyes if you like. This heart started beating before you knew you existed. Somebody, the psalm says, was paying attention even then. Feel the rhythm under your palm. Feel the breath lifting your hand a little, and letting it down. If you pray, you can say the line slowly: I am fearfully and wonderfully made. If you don't, simply feel how carefully you are put together, and let that be enough. The bell holds the time.
You knit me together. Psalm one hundred thirty-nine's picture of a life woven in secret, and known all the way down.
Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made. Today, when you catch yourself criticizing your own body or mind, stop, and handle yourself with a little awe instead. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 139 as a prayer of being known by God; its last verses, "Search me, O God," are often prayed before confession or at the end of the day.

ask God to search his own heart.

original.note: Hebrew: I was embroidered, worked with colored thread. the King James Bible says "curiously wrought".

trapdoor: what you thought: a feel-good line for a birthday card.
what it means: a person known completely, sitting, rising, fleeing, and even before birth, who ends by asking to be searched.
what a scholar hears: the verb in verse 13 can mean cover or weave, and 'curiously wrought' in verse 15 is the language of embroidery.

notes: Hebrew sakak in 139:13 (cover / weave, knit together); raqam in 139:15 (to embroider, variegate). Confirm glosses.
Year one used Psalm 139:8, 12 and 23 on other days (e.g. day 303); this day's angle is being known and woven.
